42867581.text: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.

42897081.label: Background
42897081.text: Practice guidelines recommend the use of computed tomography (CT) aortic valve calcium (AVC) scores for patients with low-gradient aortic stenosis (LG-AS). AVC has not been studied in comparison to invasive aortic valve study (IAVS).

42897081.label: Objectives
42897081.text: To determine the diagnostic performance of AVC and CT-derived aortic valve area (CT-AVA) compared to IAVS as a reference standard.

42897081.label: Methods
42897081.text: We included consecutive patients with LG-AS with echocardiography, CT and IAVS performed within 1 year at a single tertiary center. Severe AS was defined by aortic valve area (AVA) ≤1.0 cm2 measured by IAVS. CT-AVA was retrospectively measured by a blinded reader. CT-AVA and sex-based AVC were compared to AS defined by IAVS. Diagnostic performance was compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. AVC and CT-AVA were compared to cardiac events consisting of death, aortic valve replacement and cardiovascular hospitalization.

42897081.label: Results
42897081.text: Out of 294 patients in the overall cohort, 206 patients with definite AS severity by IAVS were included as the primary diagnostic cohort. Severe AS according to invasive AVA (≤1.0 cm2) was present in 72 patients (35.0%). Sex-based AVC scores had relatively poor diagnostic performance compared to the reference IAVS with AUCs of 0.59 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48-0.70) and 0.58 (95% CI 0.45-0.71) for men and women, respectively. CT-AVA had better diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.87).

42897081.label: Conclusions
42897081.text: In our study population, CT-AVA had significantly better diagnostic performance than AVC compared to the reference standard, IAVS.

42909731.label: Background
42909731.text: Radiotracer labels in positron emission tomography (PET) DICOM metadata are manually entered and often unreliable or missing, requiring expert visual verification for downstream analyses. We developed and validated deep learning models to classify PET tracers directly from image data across multiple sites and cohorts.

42909731.label: Results
42909731.text: We used PET scans obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI, n = 7429) and the Standardized Centralized Alzheimer's & Related Dementias Neuroimaging study (SCAN, n = 4869) to classify 10 tracers. We evaluated generalizability on an external test set of Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and ADRC scans containing four tracers (n = 10558). ADNI and SCAN data were combined and split into training (60%), validation (20%), and internal test (20%) sets. We trained two ConvNeXt-Large models initialized with ImageNet weights: a 10-class model (AV1451, FBP, FBP-Early, FBB, FBB-Early, FDG, MK6240, NAV4694, PI2620, PIB) and a 3-class model grouping tracers by biological target (Amyloid, FDG, Tau). Performance was evaluated using macro-F1, average precision (AP), and confusion matrices, Integrated Gradients for attribution, with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and cosine similarity to assess model interpretability and multi-cohort effects on the embedding structure. The 3-class model achieved macro-F1 ≥ 0.99 across all test sets. The 10-class model achieved macro-F1 of 0.91 on the internal test and 0.93 on the external test set where only four tracers were available. Lower performance was observed for NAV4694 (AP 0.70; misclassified as FBB, 17.2%), PI2620 (0.79; AV1451, 20.0%), and FBB (0.80; FBP, 23.3%). The attribution maps indicated the models learned some tracer specific uptake patterns as well as general imaging features. Class embeddings in the UMAP projection showed clear separation, with limited overlap among underrepresented tracers with similar binding characteristics. Cohort-level differences in learned representations were most pronounced among tau tracers, with higher within-class cosine similarity in ADNI than in SCAN (mean [SD], 0.26 [0.10] vs. 0.01 [0.06]), while amyloid tracers showed minimal shift across cohorts.

42909731.label: Conclusions
42909731.text: Classification was near-perfect when grouping tracers into three biological targets, and the 10-class model generalized well to the four tracers available in the independent external cohort. A few tracers with similar binding characteristics showed some overlap in latent space, with minimal impact on overall classification performance. Our results demonstrate that deep learning models can identify PET tracers from image appearance alone and have the potential to support semi-automated tracer identification and data curation in large multi-site PET studies.

42914181.text: [18F]fluorodihydroxyphenylalanine ([18F]DOPA) uptake is dependent on amino acid transport and decarboxylation pathways, including large neutral amino acid transporter 1, encoded by SLC7A5, which are linked to tumor aggressiveness. This study evaluated whether in vivo uptake of [18F]DOPA can serve as an imaging biomarker for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (panNETs), reflecting a tumor's transcriptional status and a patient's clinical course. Methods: This retrospective single-center study was based on a transcriptomic cohort of 74 primary panNETs. A subset of 22 panNETs from patients who underwent preoperative [18F]DOPA PET/CT constituted the discovery radiotranscriptomic cohort. [18F]DOPA tumor uptake was quantified using SUVmax and integrated with matched RNA-sequencing data. Unsupervised clustering, differential expression analysis, gene set enrichment, and tumor microenvironment deconvolution were performed to identify transcriptional programs associated with [18F]DOPA uptake. The prognostic value of SLC7A5 was evaluated in the discovery cohort, the full transcriptomic cohort (n = 74), and an independent external cohort (n = 33). Results: Unsupervised clustering of gene expression profiles identified 2 robust molecular subtypes: cluster 1 and cluster 2. Cluster 1 showed higher [18F]DOPA uptake than did cluster 2, with a median SUVmax of 24.3 versus 5.9, respectively (P = 0.030), and was associated with more advanced clinicopathologic features and shorter event-free survival. This subtype was also characterized by enrichment in extracellular matrix, stromal, vascular, and immune-related components, along with upregulation of amino acid transport and amine metabolism genes, including SLC7A5 As a mechanistic link between tracer uptake and tumor metabolism, SLC7A5 expression significantly stratified event-free survival in the discovery cohort and remained prognostic in the full cohort. Conclusion: [18F]DOPA PET uptake was associated with amino acid-driven metabolic programs in panNETs, including SLC7A5 expression, and adverse clinical features. These findings suggest that [18F]DOPA uptake may provide a noninvasive readout of tumor metabolic activity, although its value as an imaging biomarker requires independent validation.

42995281.label: Objectives
42995281.text: To compare an International Federation of Gyneology and Obstetrics (FIGO)-anchored structured MRI report with conventional narrative reporting for cervical cancer staging by evaluating referring clinicians' satisfaction.

42995281.label: Materials and methods
42995281.text: In this prospective multicentre crossover study (January-June 2024), consecutive patients with biopsy-proven cervical cancer at any FIGO stage underwent staging MRI at five European centres. For each patient, one narrative and one structured report were produced and independently evaluated by gynaecologists and radiation oncologists using a 12-item questionnaire (5-point Likert scale): five general items (Q1-Q5) for both formats and seven feature-specific items (Q6-Q12) for structured reports only. The primary endpoint was the proportion of structured-report evaluations with an overall score ≥ 20 (target ≥ 80%). Paired comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation (r) as effect size.

42995281.label: Results
42995281.text: One hundred patients were evaluated, yielding 200 report evaluations. Of 100 structured report evaluations, 98.0% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 93.0-99.8%) achieved an overall score ≥ 20, exceeding the 80% threshold, vs 78.0% (95% CI: 68.6-85.7%) for narrative reports. Structured reports scored significantly higher on all five general items and on the overall score (all p < 0.05), with the largest effects for readability (r = 0.95) and brevity (r = 0.85). The advantage was consistent across reader type, disease stage, and centre, with the strongest effect in locally advanced disease. Q6 (cervical stromal invasion) had the lowest feature-specific satisfaction (73.7% scoring ≥ 4), prompting template revision.

42995281.label: Conclusion
42995281.text: A structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging significantly outperformed narrative reporting across all quality domains in a multicentre crossover design.

42995281.label: Key points
42995281.text: Question Cervical cancer management is highly stage-dependent, yet evidence on clinician-centred benefit of structured vs narrative MRI staging reports in routine practice is scarce. Findings In a multicentre crossover study, a FIGO-anchored structured MRI report significantly outperformed narrative reporting on all five general quality domains. Clinical relevance A structured MRI report standardises the communication of staging features that drive cervical cancer management and is preferred by referring clinicians over narrative reporting across specialties, disease stages, and European centres.

43007081.text: Background Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (CA) can be misinterpreted as a benign lesion, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis; however, the effect of the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) 2022 criteria remains unverified. Purpose To retrospectively determine the frequency and outcomes of lung cancer associated with CA during screening and explore the potential effect of Lung-RADS 2022 on earlier diagnosis. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis included participants with lung cancers from three trials: the National Lung Screening Trial (2002-2007); Italian Lung Cancer Screening Trial, or ITALUNG (2004-2010); and German Lung Cancer Screening Intervention trial, or LUSI (2007-2016). Two radiologists jointly reviewed low-dose CT images to identify and morphologically characterize lung cancer associated with CA. Associations with histologic features, stage, and other variables were assessed. Lung cancer-specific survival was analyzed using Fine-Gray regression accounting for the competing risk of non-lung cancer death. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, stage, detection status, and trial. Lung-RADS 2022 criteria for atypical pulmonary cysts were applied. Results Seventy-three cancers associated with CA were identified in 1258 participants (median age, 64 years [IQR, 61-69 years]; 43 male), including 44 of 716 (6.1%) screening-detected and 29 of 542 (5.4%) non-screening-detected cancers. Multilocular morphologic type was associated with a more advanced stage than unilocular morphologic type (12 of 24 vs 15 of 49; P = .02). The 5-year lung cancer-specific survival was 51.4% (95% CI: 39.3, 62.3) for cancers associated with CA and 53.2% (95% CI: 50.1, 56.2) for 1054 participants with noncystic non-small cell lung cancer. No evidence of a difference in survival was observed (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.15 [95% CI: 0.81, 1.63]; P = .44), and results remained consistent in multivariable models. Lung-RADS 2022 might have enabled earlier diagnosis in 55 of 73 cancers associated with CA (75%). Conclusion Lung cancer associated with CA accounted for 6.1% of screening-detected and 5.4% of non-screening-detected lung cancers. Outcomes were similar to those of noncystic non-small cell lung cancer, and Lung-RADS 2022 may facilitate earlier diagnosis.

43019231.text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) have evolved from historically misclassified smooth muscle tumors to a distinct disease entity, defined by gain-of-function mutations in KIT or PDGFRA proto-oncogenes. The advent of targeted therapy for this entity in the form of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), imatinib mesylate, has transformed the treatment for GISTs, reducing recurrence and improving survival in patients with advanced disease. Radiologists play a critical role in initial lesion identification, surgical planning, and posttherapy surveillance, with cross-sectional imaging (CT and MRI) being vital in characterizing tumor features such as endophytic or exophytic nature, pseudocapsule, ulceration, necrosis, and changes in enhancement. Incorporating the Choi criteria into routine practice further refines response assessment, guiding adjustments in therapeutic strategy. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for optimal GIST management, requiring close collaboration between surgeons, oncologists, pathologists, and radiologists to establish a diagnosis, determine resectability, consider neoadjuvant or adjuvant TKIs, and monitor for disease recurrence (with imaging intervals tailored to risk classification). Future directions involve greater incorporation of molecular profiling to personalize treatments and the integration of newer-generation TKIs for imatinib-resistant cases, highlighting the continued importance of interdisciplinary coordination.

43043181.text: Background The role of endovascular treatment (EVT) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) from 24 to 96 hours after symptom onset remains uncertain. Purpose To evaluate the functional and safety outcomes of EVT versus best medical management (BMM) in patients with AIS due to large vessel occlusion (LVO) presenting greater than 24 hours to 96 hours (hereafter "24-96 hours") after symptom onset. Materials and Methods Prospectively maintained stroke registries from eight stroke centers in China (September 2020-January 2025) were analyzed in this retrospective cohort study. Patients with intracranial internal carotid artery or M1 or M2 middle cerebral artery occlusion, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 6 or higher, and Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score of 3 or higher who presented 24-96 hours after onset were included, grouped by treatment (EVT vs BMM alone), and followed for 90 days. The primary outcome was functional independence (modified Rankin Scale score of 0-2) at 90 days. Secondary safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 90-day mortality. Outcomes were compared using multivariable logistic regression and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), adjusted for demographic and clinical variables. Results Among 308 patients (mean age, 67 years ± 12 [SD]; 202 men), 205 underwent EVT and 103 received BMM. Functional independence at 90 days was more frequent with EVT than BMM (50.7% [104 of 205] vs 28.2% [29 of 103]; P < .001). After multivariable adjustment, the odds ratio (OR) for functional independence with EVT compared with BMM was 3.8 (95% CI: 2.1, 6.8; P < .001); after IPTW adjustment, the OR was 4.4 (95% CI: 2.4, 8.1; P < .001). After multivariable adjustment, the incidence of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (5.9% vs 2.9%; OR, 2.2 [95% CI: 0.6, 8.2]; P = .26) and 90-day mortality (11.2% vs 13.6%; OR, 0.6 [95% CI: 0.3, 1.4]; P = .22) did not differ between the EVT and BMM groups. Conclusion Among Chinese patients with AIS due to LVO presenting 24-96 hours after symptom onset, EVT was associated with improved functional outcomes, without clear increases in mortality or symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.

43084431.text: Pancreatic disease in pediatric patients includes a diverse range of congenital, inflammatory, traumatic, and neoplastic conditions. In this article, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of the imaging features of a broad range of pancreatic diseases in children, highlighting the roles of conventional and advanced imaging techniques while addressing pediatric-specific challenges. A structured review of pediatric pancreatic abnormalities, including the findings of US, CT, MRI with MR cholangiopancreatography, and nuclear medicine studies is presented. In addition, the benefits and limitations of these diagnostic imaging methods, as well as the necessity of a tailored, multimodality imaging paradigm for accurate diagnosis and management of pediatric pancreatic disease, are outlined. Emerging quantitative imaging methods have recently enabled objective evaluation of the pancreas at the cellular and molecular levels by means of assessment of the parenchymal volume, fat fraction, tissue stiffness, and microvascular architecture. In addition, radiomics and artificial intelligence models may enhance diagnostic accuracy by extracting large volumes of quantitative data from medical images to characterize tissue dimensions, morphology, and tissue heterogeneity. The authors provide a comprehensive review of the imaging findings of the most common neoplastic and non-neoplastic pediatric pancreatic diseases and their mimics. Finally, they outline the most common pediatric pancreatic surgical procedures, expected postoperative changes, and potential postsurgical complications to facilitate communication between the surgeon and the radiologist.
